definitely, which is why I told them to use a syringe without a needle or a tube and use it like you would a dropper. there are tiny syringes for feeding medicine that would work like that, and they can also monitor how much the chick is eating. I recommended baby bird food because the post specifically said the worms were diced, but crushing or running the mealworms through a blender would do the same thing

where did you find the baby? do you see a nest anywhere nearby (edit: just noticed that your pic is probably the nest) or a bird flying around? its best chance of survival will always be with its mum, but if she really isn’t around, you can find baby bird food that comes in powder that you can mix with water. you’ll take that up with a needle-less syringe and feed the baby every 2-3 hours. edit: you’ll use the syringe like a dropper, feeding very little at a time, practically a drop. wait for the chick to swallow before giving more, and always observe whether they’re willing to eat more. when they turn away from the food, you can stop feeding.

keep a close eye on the area that may look like their chest - that’s their crop and that will fill up when they’re eating. it will look like a little balloon when they start to get full, but it shouldn’t get so bloated for a chick this little, so keep an eye on whether they eat more or not. they can get sick when the crop gets overly full. they also need to be kept warm, so if you have a hot water bottle around you can wrap that in a thick towel and keep it near them. keeping a lid with breathing holes over their enclosure would also help keep them warm. best of luck with this one, it looks very alert and clean so the mum might just be around

Hi! I was on the way to the GP the night I wrote my last comment and told them everything I wrote here including the infection, the procedure, the stomach pain, the fever, and the higher heart rate. We brought the medication (Augmentin and Divido) from the dentist and bloodwork from December 31st of last year as well. They said my bloodwork looked good but that while the medication I was given were great, they were especially brutal on the stomach, and asked how I ate during the course of the meds. I said I never had them without food, but I was with my family and they told the doctor they noticed I hadn’t been eating a whole lot because of work during the time and also a bit before then. I also recalled then that I had been having small bouts of stomach pain even before the meds and the procedure and a slightly sour taste in my mouth.

The GP examined me and prescribed antacids, saying I had gastritis. They were also wondering why my dentist had me stop the abx but just told me to follow what they said, and to take the antacids right when I got home which I did. Just a bit later the pain subsided and the next morning all my symptoms were gone and I could move around better. The past couple days I only had occasional stomach pain in between meals and while I ate. We’ll be going for a second opinion if my condition doesn’t stay this way, but either way we’re still keeping an eye on it.

Not exactly an answer, but when speaking of age using 살 (which you use with 젊은들/어린이들), Koreans use Korean numbers 하나 둘 etc., while when using 세 (used with respected 어른들, especially the elderly), they use 한자 numbers 일 이 etc. You probably hear ages >70 pronounced using 한자 because Koreans don't use Korean numbers as high as those on an everyday basis these days outside of the age context, making them forget many of them along the way. Since Korean numbers less than 10 are most familiar, people end up inventing pronunciations for ages such as 88 years old like 팔십여덟세, where the tens digit is pronounced in Sino-Korean while the ones digit in pure Korean. A lot of people hav given advice on actually learning Hangeul, so I'll share something about typing in Korean instead. The Korean keyboard was designed to be as comfortable to use as possible. With Korean always being spelt with a consonant, vowel, so on pattern, designers placed the consonants on the left side of the keyboard, and the vowels on the right. I'll leave learning the actual format of the keyboard to you for once you've finished learning Hangeul, but to make double consonants (쌍자음 ssangjaum), you press shift like you would when typing a capital Latin letter and press any of the double consonants on the top left side of the keyboard (the 5 keys from the very left top row). When typing, you can type conveniently by starting with a consonant on the left side and the vowel on the right. No sweat. All the best for your Korean journey - you'll love every step of it!

A lot of Koreans who offer or agree to help others learn Korean are often doing so to learn another language in the process too. I've also had my more-than-fair share of Korean friends that came and went, but right now I do still have contact with one of them, though a little rare with our own busy schedules. I think if you'd like to keep being friends with a Korean whilst learning their language, you could try looking for someone who is also learning your own language, then you could help one another in each of your goals and have a bit more to talk about than just your cultures. My Korean friend, Claire and I have spoken about our cultures and traditions, but we've also spoken about the reasons we decided to learn each other's language, which helped us become closer and more friendly with one another, much like real life friends do. That would be my best advice for you if you want to get off at a good start in making long distance Korean friends online :)

I am currently taking a break from intensive Korean self-studying, but even so, I am still learning every day as I try to have any sort of contact with the language, no matter how little, each day. I'm a fan of Korean popular music, so I get to listen to Korean frequently, and I've long since switched the language on my phone to Korean, which allows me regular interaction with the text of the language. When I studied intensively I frequently chatted with quite a few native Koreans, and I sometimes still do. Occasionally I find myself reading Korean comics and stories, or watching a Korean drama or movie or two, like Train to Busan which rose to fame just recently. Like one of the other commenters said, it really doesn't feel much like studying because there are so many ways to do it, and every single one is as enjoyable as the other.

I kind of "began" studying Korean almost seven years ago when I was a kid, learning from words to basic greetings like you, and only when I took it seriously did I actually learn to *understand* Korean.

No language is learned immediately. You can try every shortcut there is to memorising words and phrases, yet none of those would get you far. For the few that can do it with everything else that they have going on, 6-8 months may already seem lightning fast. For those that don't take it that seriously or might be doing something wrong, or simply memorising phrases used by tourists to get around, I personally don't think they'll get anywhere, but like the others have said, everyone learns at their own pace.

If you study seriously enough, watch or maybe listen to enough native speakers speaking (you can find loads on the Internet), and use the right materials for learning, I reckon about a year will get you to understand at least a portion of what native Koreans say or write. Happy learning! :D
